analysis.one_liner: Lets states run coal ash permits instead of the EPA, weakening enforcement and delaying cleanup of leaking ash ponds.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 258-166 on July 22, 2015, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal ash is the toxic waste left over from burning coal at power plants, and it sits in large ponds and landfills that can leak into groundwater. In 2015 the EPA issued the first-ever national rule requiring utilities to monitor groundwater, meet structural safety standards, and close leaking unlined ash ponds. This bill would have let each state choose to run its own coal ash permit program instead, with the state holding sole enforcement power, longer deadlines, and the ability to modify federal definitions and standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired power plants, chiefly electric utilities, which would get longer timelines, state-run permits, and no concurrent federal enforcement over ash ponds and landfills. Coal mining companies would benefit from the exclusion of ash placed at mine reclamation sites from any federal program. Companies that use coal ash in fill and other products would benefit from exemptions for those uses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal-fired utilities and coal mining companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces direct EPA regulation of coal ash with state-run permit programs; the state that adopts a program gets sole enforcement authority, and the EPA may not enforce concurrently [S2][S4][S5].

Unlined surface impoundments may be allowed to keep operating until 102 months after enactment, and even beyond that date as long as they meet a groundwater protection standard, rather than being required to close on the EPA rule's schedule [S5].

The implementing agency may authorize alternative groundwater protection standards, may use an alternative point of compliance, and may determine that corrective action is not necessary, using the more lenient landfill provisions of part 258 rather than the coal ash rule's [S5].
A state agency may change the federal definitions used in the coal ash rule, needing only to provide a 'reasonable basis' in its certification [S5].
A federal EPA permit program may not apply to the use, placement, and storage of coal ash at coal mining and reclamation operations [S2][S5].
If any provision of the EPA's coal ash rule conflicts with the bill, the bill controls, and the EPA rule may be implemented only through this permit program [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near coal ash ponds and landfills, especially those relying on groundwater, would bear the risk of weaker state oversight, longer operation of unlined ponds, and gaps in federal enforcement. Taxpayers could also pay more if state programs fail and EPA has to build programs from scratch under the bill's slower deficiency process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near coal ash disposal sites

drawbacks.text: The bill lets unlined ash ponds — ponds with no liner to keep toxins out of groundwater — keep operating for years longer than the EPA rule required, and even beyond the bill's own deadline if they meet a groundwater standard [S5].

A state that adopts the program holds sole enforcement authority, and the EPA is barred from concurrent enforcement, so residents' protection depends entirely on the willingness and capacity of one state agency [S5].

State agencies may rewrite the federal rule's definitions and may relax groundwater standards or forgo corrective action in particular cases, with federal review available only through a lengthy deficiency-notice process that starts with giving the state a chance to fix things [S5].
Broad exemptions for 'beneficial use' and structural fill mean large quantities of ash could be placed on land outside the permit program's main requirements [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not a repeal: state permit programs would have to incorporate most of the EPA rule's criteria — design, groundwater monitoring and corrective action, closure, financial assurance, dust controls, and inspections — and citizen suits are preserved [S4][S5]. Supporters argued a permit system with state expertise would work better than the rule's self-implementing requirements [S2]. But the bill's actual pull is toward delay and discretion: longer deadlines for unlined ponds, weaker groundwater provisions, state-set definitions, and no federal backup enforcement. Set against the reason the EPA rule exists in the first place — failures like the 2008 Tennessee spill that dumped coal ash across rivers and homes — the trade tilts toward the utilities writing the checks for cleanup, and away from the people drinking the groundwater.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House with a big vote, sat in the Senate for nearly a year before being referred to committee, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported by a 32-19 vote in April 2015 and reported it in June [S7].
The House passed it on July 22, 2015, 258-166, with 239 of 245 Republicans voting yes and 19 of 188 Democrats [S7][S9].
A Democratic motion to recommit — requiring disposal sites to prevent groundwater and drinking water contamination, including the Great Lakes — failed 184-240 along party lines [S7][S8].

The Senate received the bill on July 23, 2015, referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee on July 14, 2016, and took no further action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S7].
Because the bill never became law, the EPA's 2015 coal ash rule — which this bill would have replaced as the sole vehicle for implementation — remained the governing framework [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA rule's federal standards stayed in place, so communities near coal ash sites kept stronger protections than the bill would have allowed, and utilities did not get the state-run, enforcement-light permit program they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal ash communities; utilities got nothing

sides.party_line_note: Passage was 239-1 among Republicans and 19-165 among Democrats, and the motion to recommit split 184-0 Democrats to 0-240 Republicans; four House Democrats cosponsored [S6][S8][S9].

industries.note: The bill would have given utilities state-run permits, sole state enforcement, longer deadlines for unlined ash ponds, and relaxed groundwater provisions — a lower cost of compliance with the 2015 EPA rule. Those savings come at the price of continued risk of ash leaking into groundwater near disposal sites.

The bill exempts the placement and storage of coal ash at surface and underground mine reclamation operations from any federal permit program, opening a disposal outlet outside the bill's requirements.

industries.industry: Coal ash recycling and beneficial-use firms
industries.note: Exemptions for engineered structural fill, raw-material storage, and beneficial uses that substitute for virgin material would remove those uses from the permit program, lowering costs. Recycling ash instead of ponding it can be environmentally positive, but the exemptions could also allow large on-land ash deposits with less oversight.
